## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds, so any non-zero score is useful signal. Two things could explain the zero. (1) Too few updates: the default recipe gives only about 32 updates of 4096 samples. (2) A weak bias for where a brick lands. A placement is correct only if every footprint cell at the landing layer (the maximum column height under the footprint) is a missing target cell, and no target cell below gets sealed. The current head squeezes all layers into channels, so it has to learn a height-indexed lookup. An exact build needs every step right, so per-step accuracy has to be very high. I propose a 2x2 design over {current network, layer-wise head} × {default recipe, recipe with more updates}. The starting result fills the fourth cell. This separates the effect of the network from that of the recipe. All candidates stay at or below the starting network's compute, so the sample budget does not shrink.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success, the same as the starting network. That includes the layer-wise gated head, a recipe with about 1.8x more steps and updates, and the two combined. So neither change alone was enough, and we have no gradient to follow. A likely cause is the placement head. Max, min and average pooling over the footprint cannot express a rule like "the landing layer L is the maximum height under the footprint, and every cell under the footprint has a missing target cell at L". That needs features from each cell in the footprint kept separate. Next I test a head that gathers each footprint cell's learned features separately and feeds them to an MLP. I pair it with a recipe change: lower entropy and more updates. A third candidate guards against the world differing from its description by adding the legality mask as an input and a non-spatial fully connected logit path.

### Round 3
After six trials, every one has scored exactly 0 on dev and also 0 on training success. That covers three head designs (pooled, layer-gated and footprint-gather) and recipes running from 106k to 242k steps. Seed noise can't explain this, and neither can the recipe. The starting network also scored 0, which points to the world itself breaking something that all these designs share. The note says the world may differ from its description. What every design so far has in common is that it scores each action from features at that action's own grid location. If the real link between action index and cell is a transpose, a flip or a permutation, translation-equivariant conv heads cannot learn it. The FC path in r2c3 was a weak test: it started at zero, sat beside a dominant conv head and got only 106k steps. This round therefore tests heads that do not assume the mapping: a conv head that mixes all 8 rotations and flips, a fully connected head, and a head that learns per-action attention over cells.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0, on dev and in training, across very different heads (pooled, layer-gated, footprint-gather, dihedral, dense FC, per-action attention). So the bottleneck is probably not how actions map to cells. The likely causes are learning speed and precision. An exact build needs roughly 10 to 30 correct placements in a row, then DONE at exactly the right moment, and every run so far had only 32 to 120 policy updates. Recipe space is barely explored: only 2- and 4-epoch runs with 128 or 256 envs. The program says ppo_epochs=1 gives about 3.25x more environment steps, and that is untested. DONE has always been scored from weak mean/max pooling of trunk features. A learned per-cell projection followed by amax could better detect "anything still missing". This last round bets on more samples and policy updates, a sharper DONE and value signal, small-init output layers, and one global-attention variant.
